note: 50 mixed-form items across the chapter's concepts. Difficulty 17 Easy / 17 Medium / 16 Hard.

items.stem: What is a magnetic field?
items.answer: A magnetic field is the region around a magnet or a current-carrying conductor within which a magnetic force can be detected. It has both magnitude and direction at every point.

items.stem: Why do two magnetic field lines never intersect?
items.answer: If two lines crossed, there would be two different directions of the field at the point of intersection, and a compass needle placed there would have to point two ways at once, which is impossible.

items.stem: How does an electromagnet differ from a permanent magnet?
items.answer: An electromagnet is magnetic only while a current flows and its strength can be varied or switched off, whereas a permanent magnet retains its magnetism and its strength cannot be adjusted.

items.stem: What is the shape of the magnetic field around a long straight current-carrying wire?
items.answer: The field lines form concentric circles in a plane perpendicular to the wire, centred on the wire. They are closer together near the wire, showing that the field is stronger there and weakens with distance.

items.stem: Name the three wires in a domestic supply and give the function of each.
items.answer: The live wire, usually red or brown, carries the current at high potential. The neutral wire, usually black or blue, is at earth potential and completes the circuit. The earth wire, green or green and yellow, connects the metal casing of an appliance to the earth as a safety measure.

items.stem: Why is a fuse always placed in the live wire?
items.answer: So that when it melts it disconnects the appliance from the high potential. If it were placed in the neutral wire, the fuse could blow while the appliance remained connected to the live supply and therefore still dangerous to touch.

items.stem: Why does a current-carrying solenoid behave like a bar magnet?
items.answer: The circular fields of the individual turns combine so that the field lines emerge from one end and enter the other, running in parallel inside. The pattern is indistinguishable from that of a bar magnet, so one end behaves as a north pole and the other as a south pole.

items.stem: Why is earthing essential for a metal-bodied appliance but less critical for a plastic-bodied one?
items.answer: If the live wire touches a metal body, the whole casing becomes live and anyone touching it receives a shock. Earthing gives that current a low-resistance path to the ground, which also blows the fuse. A plastic body is an insulator, so it cannot become live in the same way, though the internal wiring still needs protection.

items.stem: State four properties of magnetic field lines.
items.answer: First, outside a magnet they run from the north pole to the south pole, and inside the magnet they continue from south to north, so every line forms a closed loop. Second, they never intersect one another, because two directions of the field at one point is impossible and a compass needle cannot point two ways at once. Third, the spacing of the lines indicates the strength of the field: where they are crowded the field is strong, as near a pole, and where they are far apart it is weak. Fourth, the tangent to a line at any point gives the direction of the field there, which is the direction in which the north end of a compass needle would point. A fifth point worth adding is that field lines are a representation rather than physical objects; they are a way of recording the magnitude and direction of the field at every point in a single picture.

items.stem: State the right-hand thumb rule and explain how to apply it to a straight wire.
items.answer: The rule states that if a current-carrying conductor is imagined to be held in the right hand with the thumb pointing along the direction of the current, then the direction in which the fingers curl round the conductor gives the direction of the magnetic field lines. To apply it to a straight vertical wire carrying current upwards, hold the right hand with the thumb pointing up along the wire. The fingers then curl anticlockwise when viewed from above, so the field lines are anticlockwise circles around the wire as seen from above. If the current is reversed to flow downwards, the thumb points down and the fingers curl the other way, so the field lines become clockwise as seen from above. The rule is also called Maxwell's corkscrew rule, since a right-handed screw advancing in the direction of the current turns in the direction of the field. It is used only for finding the field produced by a current, and should not be confused with Fleming's rules, which concern force and induced current.

items.stem: Describe how to make an electromagnet and state three ways of increasing its strength.
items.answer: Take a long insulated copper wire and wind it into many closely spaced turns around a soft iron rod, forming a solenoid with the rod as its core. Connect the ends of the wire through a switch to a battery. When the current flows, the iron rod becomes strongly magnetised and behaves as a bar magnet with a north pole at one end and a south pole at the other; when the current is switched off the magnetism almost disappears, since soft iron does not retain it. Three ways of increasing the strength are to increase the current through the coil, since the field of each turn grows with the current; to increase the number of turns per unit length, since the fields of the turns add; and to use a soft iron core rather than air, since iron concentrates the field lines greatly. Reversing the current reverses the poles without changing the strength. The soft iron core is chosen deliberately: steel would retain its magnetism and the device could not be switched off, which is exactly what an electromagnet must be able to do.

items.stem: State Fleming's left-hand rule and explain how it is used in an electric motor.
items.answer: Stretch the thumb, the forefinger and the middle finger of the left hand so that all three are mutually perpendicular. If the forefinger points in the direction of the magnetic field and the middle finger in the direction of the current, then the thumb points in the direction of the force acting on the conductor, and hence the direction in which it moves. In an electric motor a rectangular coil carrying current is placed between the poles of a magnet. Consider the two sides of the coil that lie perpendicular to the field. In one of them the current flows one way and in the other it flows the opposite way, since the current goes round the loop. Applying the rule to each side separately gives forces in opposite directions, one upward and one downward. These two opposite forces on opposite sides of the axis constitute a couple, which turns the coil. When the coil has turned half a revolution, the two sides have exchanged places and the forces would now oppose the rotation, so a split-ring commutator reverses the current at that moment and keeps the couple acting in the same rotational sense. The motor therefore continues to turn in one direction.

items.stem: Describe the wiring of a domestic electric circuit and the safety devices included in it.
items.answer: The supply reaches the house through a main fuse and a meter, then goes to a distribution box from which separate circuits run. Typically one circuit of 15 A is provided for heavy appliances such as geysers and air conditioners, and another of 5 A for lights and fans, since the two need different current capacities. Within each circuit the appliances are connected in parallel between the live and neutral wires, so that each receives the full supply voltage, each can be switched independently, and a failure in one does not affect the others. Each socket and each appliance is controlled by its own switch, which is always placed in the live wire so that switching off actually disconnects the appliance from the high potential. Three safety devices are included. A fuse or a miniature circuit breaker is fitted in the live wire of each circuit, and melts or trips if the current becomes dangerously large, whether through overloading or a short circuit. The earth wire connects the metal body of each appliance to a metal plate buried in the ground, so that if the live wire touches the casing the current flows harmlessly to earth and blows the fuse instead of passing through a person. Proper insulation and correctly rated cables complete the protection.

items.stem: Distinguish overloading from short-circuiting, and explain how a fuse deals with each.
items.answer: The two are different faults with the same symptom of excessive current. Overloading occurs when too many appliances are operated from the same circuit at once, or when a single appliance draws more current than the circuit was designed to carry. The wiring is intact and the current, though excessive, is limited by the total resistance of the appliances in parallel. It builds up gradually as more appliances are switched on, and its cause is a mistake of use rather than a fault of equipment. A drop in supply voltage can contribute, since some appliances then draw more current to deliver their rated power. Short-circuiting occurs when the live and neutral wires come into direct contact, usually because the insulation has failed or a wire has been damaged. The current now bypasses the appliance altogether and flows through a path of almost no resistance, so by Ohm's law it becomes enormous, far larger than any overload, and it does so instantaneously. A fuse deals with both by the same mechanism, since both present it with a current above its rating: the heat produced follows I squared R t, so the fuse wire melts and breaks the circuit. The difference is in timing. An overload heats the fuse steadily until it melts, which may take a second or more, while a short circuit blows it almost at once because the current is so much larger. In both cases the fuse must be rated just above the normal working current of the circuit, and must never be replaced by a thicker wire, since that would let a fault current pass into the fixed wiring inside the walls where the heating cannot be seen.

items.stem: Explain how the magnetic field around a straight conductor depends on the current and the distance, and how this can be shown.
items.answer: The field at a point near a straight conductor is directly proportional to the current flowing and inversely proportional to the distance from the wire. To show the dependence on distance, place a compass needle at various distances from a wire carrying a steady current and note the deflection. The deflection is large close to the wire and becomes progressively smaller as the compass is moved away, showing that the field weakens with distance. The same conclusion follows from a picture of the field lines: sprinkling iron filings on a card through which a current-carrying wire passes vertically shows concentric circles that are crowded near the wire and widely spaced further out, and crowding of lines represents a strong field. To show the dependence on current, keep the compass at a fixed distance and increase the current using a rheostat. The deflection increases as the current grows, and reversing the current reverses the deflection, which also confirms that the direction of the field depends on the direction of the current as the right-hand thumb rule predicts. Two practical points follow from these relations. Bringing a conductor closer to a compass or increasing its current are the two ways of strengthening the effect. And because the field falls off with distance, the field of a single straight wire is weak at any useful distance, which is why a coil or solenoid is used when a strong field is wanted: it places many turns of wire close together so that their contributions add.

items.stem: Explain why a current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field experiences a force, and what determines its size and direction.
items.answer: A current is a flow of charge, and a moving charge in a magnetic field experiences a force. In a conductor, the individual charges cannot leave the wire, so the forces on them are transmitted to the conductor as a whole, which therefore experiences a force. Equivalently, the current produces its own magnetic field, and the interaction between that field and the external field results in a force on the conductor. The size of the force depends on three things: it increases with the current, with the strength of the external field, and with the length of conductor lying in the field. It also depends on the angle between the conductor and the field, being greatest when the two are perpendicular and zero when they are parallel; in the parallel case the conductor's own circular field lies along the external field and there is no interaction to produce a force. The direction is given by Fleming's left-hand rule, with the forefinger along the field, the middle finger along the current and the thumb giving the force, and it is perpendicular to both the field and the current. Two consequences are worth drawing. Reversing either the current or the field reverses the force, while reversing both leaves it unchanged, which is precisely why a motor needs a commutator. And since the force is perpendicular to the current, the effect converts electrical energy into mechanical motion rather than merely into heat, which is the basis of the electric motor, the loudspeaker and the moving-coil galvanometer.

items.stem: Assertion (A): A compass needle near a current-carrying wire is deflected. Reason (R): A current produces a magnetic field around itself. Choose the correct option.
items.explanation: Both are true, and the field produced by the current is exactly what acts on the needle.

Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
options.why: The field produced by the current is precisely the cause of the deflection.

options.text: A is true but R is false
options.why: A current genuinely produces a magnetic field, as Oersted found.

options.text: A is false but R is true
options.why: The deflection is readily observed and was the original discovery.

items.stem: Assertion (A): Two magnetic field lines can intersect. Reason (R): The tangent to a field line gives the direction of the field. Choose the correct option.
items.explanation: The reason is true and is exactly what defeats the assertion: an intersection would give two directions at one point.

options.text: A is false but R is true
Both A and R are true and R explains A

options.text: Both A and R are false
options.why: The tangent genuinely gives the direction of the field.

options.text: A is true but R is false
options.why: A compass needle cannot point two ways at once.

items.explanation: The reason is true and is exactly why the assertion is dangerous: the fault current then passes into the fixed wiring instead of being interrupted.

Both A and R are true and R explains A
options.why: Carrying more current is the reason it is dangerous, not the reason it is advisable.

items.explanation: Both are true, and losing magnetism on switching off is exactly the property an electromagnet requires.

options.text: Both A and R are true and R explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
options.why: Being switchable is precisely the point of an electromagnet.

options.text: A is true but R is false
options.why: Soft iron genuinely retains almost no magnetism.

options.text: A is false but R is true
options.why: Soft iron is the standard core material for an electromagnet.

items.stem: State whether true or false: a magnetic field has both magnitude and direction.
items.explanation: The field is a vector quantity, which is why field lines carry arrows.

options.why: It is a vector quantity, specified by both a strength and a direction.

items.stem: State whether true or false: reversing the current reverses the direction of the magnetic field around a wire.
items.explanation: By the right-hand thumb rule, reversing the thumb reverses the way the fingers curl.

options.why: The field direction follows the current direction, so reversing one reverses the other.

items.stem: State whether true or false: domestic appliances are connected in series.
items.explanation: They are connected in parallel, so each gets the full voltage and can be switched independently.

options.why: Parallel connection is used, so one failure does not stop the rest.

items.stem: State whether true or false: a conductor placed parallel to a magnetic field experiences the maximum force.
items.explanation: The force is zero when the conductor is parallel to the field and maximum when it is perpendicular.

options.why: Parallel gives zero force; perpendicular gives the maximum.

items.stem: The rule giving the direction of the magnetic field around a current is the ___________ thumb rule.
items.answer: right-hand

items.stem: The core of an electromagnet is made of ___________ iron.
items.answer: soft

items.stem: In Fleming's left-hand rule the thumb gives the direction of the ___________.
items.answer: force, and hence the motion

items.stem: When the live and neutral wires touch each other directly, the fault is called a ___________.
items.answer: short circuit

items.stem: Describe the magnetic effect of an electric current and how it was discovered, and give the field patterns for the three standard arrangements.
items.answer: The magnetic effect of an electric current is the production of a magnetic field in the space around a conductor whenever a current flows through it. It was discovered by Oersted, who noticed that a compass needle placed near a wire was deflected when a current was switched on and returned to its original position when the current was stopped, and that reversing the current reversed the deflection. This showed that electricity and magnetism are connected, and it was the beginning of the subject of electromagnetism. Three arrangements give three characteristic patterns. Around a long straight conductor, the field lines are concentric circles lying in a plane perpendicular to the wire and centred on it, crowded near the wire and spaced further apart with distance, showing that the field weakens as one moves away. Their direction is given by the right-hand thumb rule. Around a circular loop, each small part of the wire contributes a circular field, and at the centre all these contributions point the same way, so the field there is strong and directed along the axis of the loop; the field is greatest at the centre and falls off away from it. Inside a solenoid, which is a long coil of many turns, the fields of the turns combine to give a uniform field with parallel lines along the axis, while outside the pattern is that of a bar magnet, with lines emerging from one end and entering the other. This last arrangement is used to make electromagnets.

items.stem: Explain the three faults that can occur in a domestic circuit and the precautions that guard against each.
items.answer: The first fault is overloading. Too many appliances are run from one circuit, or an appliance draws more current than the circuit was designed for, so the current exceeds the safe value and the wiring overheats. A fall in supply voltage can contribute, since some appliances then draw a larger current to deliver their rated power. The precautions are to provide separate circuits of appropriate rating, typically a 15 A circuit for heavy appliances and a 5 A circuit for lights and fans, to avoid running many high-power appliances from one socket, and to fit a correctly rated fuse or circuit breaker which interrupts the supply before the wiring is damaged. The second fault is short-circuiting. The live and neutral wires come into direct contact, usually because the insulation has perished or a cable has been damaged, so the current bypasses the appliance and flows through a path of almost no resistance. The current becomes enormous almost instantly and can start a fire. The precautions are sound insulation, cables of adequate thickness, careful workmanship, and again a fuse, which blows at once under such a current. The third fault is a live casing. The live wire touches the metal body of an appliance, so that the whole casing is at high potential and anyone touching it receives a severe shock. The precaution is earthing: the metal body is connected by the green earth wire to a metal plate buried in the ground, so a fault current flows harmlessly to earth and also blows the fuse. Three general precautions apply throughout: switches must always be placed in the live wire so that switching off genuinely disconnects the appliance, the fuse must be in the live wire for the same reason, and a fuse must never be replaced by a thicker wire, since that moves the weakest point of the circuit into the fixed wiring inside the walls where overheating cannot be seen.

items.stem: Explain why a solenoid produces a strong uniform field inside it while a single straight wire does not, and how this is exploited.
items.answer: The field of a single straight wire consists of concentric circles around it, and its strength falls off inversely with distance. Two limitations follow. The field is weak except very close to the wire, and it is not uniform, since both its direction and its magnitude change from point to point. Neither property is useful for magnetising something. A solenoid overcomes both by geometry rather than by any new physics. It is a long coil of many closely wound turns. Consider a point well inside it. Every turn contributes a field, and because the current goes the same way round in each turn, all those contributions point the same way along the axis. The contributions therefore add rather than partly cancelling, so many turns produce a field many times stronger than one. At the same time, the contributions of the turns on either side of the point combine in such a way that the resulting field is very nearly the same in magnitude and direction everywhere well inside the coil, so the field is uniform and the lines are parallel. Outside the solenoid the lines emerge from one end and return to the other, giving exactly the pattern of a bar magnet, so one end behaves as a north pole and the other as a south pole. This is exploited to make electromagnets. Placing a soft iron rod inside the solenoid strengthens the field greatly, because the iron concentrates the field lines, and soft iron is chosen rather than steel because it loses almost all its magnetism when the current stops, which is precisely what makes the magnet switchable. The strength can be raised by increasing the current or the number of turns per unit length, and the poles can be reversed by reversing the current. Such electromagnets are used in electric bells, in relays, in loudspeakers, in cranes for lifting scrap iron, and in medical scanners, all applications that need a magnet whose strength can be controlled or which can be turned off, and none of which a permanent magnet could serve.

items.stem: Describe the construction and working of an electric motor, and explain the function of the commutator.
items.answer: An electric motor converts electrical energy into mechanical energy. It consists of a rectangular coil of insulated copper wire, called the armature, mounted so that it can rotate on an axle between the poles of a strong magnet. The two ends of the coil are joined to the two halves of a split metal ring, the commutator, and two carbon brushes press against these halves and carry the current from the battery. Working: when the current flows, the two sides of the coil that lie perpendicular to the field each experience a force. Because the current flows in opposite directions in these two sides, the forces act in opposite directions, one pushing that side up and the other pushing the opposite side down, as Fleming's left-hand rule confirms when applied to each side separately. Two equal and opposite forces acting on opposite sides of the axle form a couple, and the coil turns. The function of the commutator is the crucial point. After the coil has turned through half a revolution, the two sides have exchanged places. If the current continued in the same direction through the coil, the forces would now act so as to turn it back, and the coil would simply oscillate about the vertical position rather than rotate. The split ring solves this: at exactly the half-revolution position the two brushes change contact from one half of the ring to the other, which reverses the direction of the current through the coil. The force on each side is therefore reversed just as the side changes position, so the couple continues to act in the same rotational sense and the coil keeps turning in one direction. In short, the commutator reverses the current every half turn so that a steady rotation is produced from a steady supply. Practical motors are made more powerful by using many turns of wire, a soft iron core to concentrate the field, and several coils set at angles so that the couple never falls to zero.

items.stem: A 5 A circuit is supplied at 220 V. Find the maximum power it can safely carry.
items.answer: Power equals voltage times current, that is 220 times 5, which is 1100 W. So appliances totalling more than about 1100 W on this circuit would overload it, which is why heavy appliances are placed on a separate 15 A circuit.

items.stem: A 220 V circuit fitted with a 5 A fuse is used for a 1000 W heater and four 100 W lamps. Determine whether the fuse will blow.
items.answer: Total power demanded is 1000 plus 4 times 100, which is 1000 plus 400, that is 1400 W. The current drawn is power divided by voltage, that is 1400 divided by 220, which is about 6.4 A. This exceeds the 5 A rating of the fuse, so the fuse will blow. To use these appliances together, either the heater should be moved to a 15 A circuit or fewer lamps should be run on this one. Note that the calculation assumes all the appliances are on at once, which is exactly the condition under which overloading occurs.

items.stem: An appliance of resistance 44 ohms runs on 220 V. A fault reduces the circuit resistance to 2 ohms. Compare the currents and the heating, and comment.
items.answer: Normally the current is I equals V divided by R, that is 220 divided by 44, which is 5 A. Under the fault the current is 220 divided by 2, which is 110 A. The current has therefore risen by a factor of 110 divided by 5, that is 22 times. The heating, however, follows I squared R t, and comparing the rates of heat production in the two cases gives a factor of 110 squared times 2, divided by 5 squared times 44, that is 24200 divided by 1100, which is 22. So the rate of heat production in the circuit also rises about 22 times. The comment worth making is twofold. First, this is why a short circuit is so dangerous and so immediate: a current 22 times the working value appears the instant the fault occurs, and the heat is dissipated wherever the resistance happens to lie, including in the fixed wiring. Second, it is why the fuse must be rated only slightly above the normal 5 A; a fuse rated at 15 A would still blow here, but one replaced by a thick wire might carry 110 A long enough to set the insulation alight.

items.stem: Match each arrangement in Column I with its field pattern in Column II. Column I: (a) straight conductor, (b) circular loop, (c) long solenoid, (d) bar magnet. Column II: (i) uniform parallel lines inside, (ii) concentric circles round the wire, (iii) lines from north pole to south pole outside, (iv) lines along the axis at the centre.
items.answer: (a) straight conductor - (ii) concentric circles round the wire. (b) circular loop - (iv) lines along the axis at the centre. (c) long solenoid - (i) uniform parallel lines inside. (d) bar magnet - (iii) lines from north pole to south pole outside.

items.stem: Match each wire or device in Column I with its function in Column II. Column I: (a) live wire, (b) neutral wire, (c) earth wire, (d) fuse. Column II: (i) melts to break the circuit on excess current, (ii) carries current at high potential, (iii) safely conducts fault current to the ground, (iv) completes the circuit at earth potential.
items.answer: (a) live wire - (ii) carries current at high potential. (b) neutral wire - (iv) completes the circuit at earth potential. (c) earth wire - (iii) safely conducts fault current to the ground. (d) fuse - (i) melts to break the circuit on excess current.

items.stem: Draw a labelled diagram of the magnetic field around a straight current-carrying conductor and state how the direction is found.
items.answer: Draw a horizontal card or sheet with a vertical wire passing through a hole at its centre, and mark the wire clearly. Show the wire connected below to a battery and a key, and mark an arrow on the wire indicating the direction of the current, taking it as flowing upwards. On the surface of the card, draw several concentric circles centred on the wire, drawn close together near the wire and progressively further apart as the radius increases. Put an arrowhead on each circle to show the direction of the field, anticlockwise as seen from above for an upward current. Label the circles magnetic field lines, and annotate that their crowding near the wire shows the field is stronger there and weakens with distance. Draw a small compass needle resting on the card at two different radii, and show it aligned along the tangent to the circle at each position, with a larger deflection at the smaller radius. Beside the diagram, state how the direction is found: apply the right-hand thumb rule by imagining the wire grasped in the right hand with the thumb pointing along the current, whereupon the curled fingers give the direction of the field lines. Add a final annotation that reversing the current reverses the arrowheads on every circle, which can be checked by reversing the battery and watching the compass needles swing through 180 degrees.

items.stem: Draw a labelled diagram of an electric motor and annotate the function of each part.
items.answer: Draw two magnet poles facing each other, labelling the left one N and the right one S, and draw horizontal field lines running from N to S across the gap. Between them draw a rectangular coil mounted on a horizontal axle, and label it armature coil. Mark arrows on the coil showing the current flowing round the loop, so that the arrow on the near side points one way and the arrow on the far side points the opposite way. At one end of the axle draw a metal ring split into two halves with a gap between them, and label it split-ring commutator. Draw two carbon blocks pressing against the two halves and label them brushes, connecting them by wires to a battery and a key. Now annotate each part. Against the magnet, note that it provides the uniform external field. Against the coil, note that it carries the current and experiences the forces. Against the two sides of the coil, apply Fleming's left-hand rule and mark the resulting force with an upward arrow on one side and a downward arrow on the other, annotating that these two opposite forces on opposite sides of the axle form a couple that turns the coil. Against the commutator, note the key function: after half a revolution the two sides of the coil have exchanged places, so the brushes change contact from one half of the ring to the other and reverse the current through the coil, which keeps the couple acting in the same rotational sense. Add a note that without the commutator the coil would merely oscillate rather than rotate. Against the brushes, note that they maintain contact with the rotating commutator while remaining stationary. Finally annotate the energy conversion: electrical energy into mechanical energy of rotation.

items.stem: Describe an experiment proving that an electric current produces a magnetic field, and show that the field depends on the current.
items.answer: Fix a horizontal sheet of cardboard and pass a straight copper wire vertically through a hole at its centre, connecting the wire below through a key and a rheostat to a battery, with an ammeter in series to read the current. Place several small compass needles on the card at different distances from the wire, and note that with the key open they all point north, along the earth's field. Now close the key. Every compass needle swings away from north and takes up a position along the tangent to a circle centred on the wire, the needles nearer the wire being deflected further. Open the key and the needles return to north. Repeat with the battery connections reversed, and every needle swings to the opposite tangential direction. The first conclusion follows. A deflection appears only while the current flows, disappears when it stops, and reverses when the current reverses. Since nothing else has changed, the current must be producing a magnetic field, and its direction depends on the direction of the current. Confirm the shape of the field by sprinkling iron filings evenly on the card and tapping it gently while the current flows: the filings settle into concentric circles centred on the wire, crowded near it and spaced further out. Now show the dependence on current. Keep one compass at a fixed distance from the wire and use the rheostat to increase the current in steps, recording the ammeter reading and the angle of deflection each time. The deflection increases steadily as the current increases, showing that the strength of the field grows with the current. The fixed distance matters here, because the field also falls off with distance, which is separately demonstrated by the greater deflection of the nearer needles in the first part of the experiment. Two features are essential to the proof. The needles must be observed with the key both open and closed, since only the change on switching establishes that the current and not some other object is the cause. And the reversal test is what rules out heating or vibration as the explanation, since neither would reverse when the battery is turned round.
